newsitem.title: FRANCE: Serbia, Bosnia agree full diplomatic links.
newsitem.headline: Serbia, Bosnia agree full diplomatic links.

text.p: Serbia and Bosnia agreed on Thursday to open full diplomatic relations and solve the burning post-war issue of the succession of former Yugoslavia, French President Jacques Chirac said.

Chirac told a news conference after talks in Paris between former foes Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia that the two heads of state "agreed to establish full diplomatic relations and exchange ambassadors very soon".

In an agreement signed at Chirac's Elysee presidential palace, Bosnia accepted the continuity of Yugoslavia as the successor state to the former Yugoslav republic, and Yugoslavia agreed in return to respect the integrity of Bosnia.
The talks also produced bilateral agreements on trade, customs union and freedom of movement between the two countries without visas.
Milosevic and Izetbegovic, the newly-elected leader of Bosnia's three-man presidency, held two rounds of talks and had lunch with Chirac before signing the eight-article agreement and shaking hands.
"I think everything has been said in the document we have signed here today. Now we have to implement it," Izetbegovic said.

"We have taken a crucial step forward towards a total stability regarding the political situation in the region," Milosevic said. "I am deeply convinced that we will succeed in achieving what we have set out to do and what is indeed in the best interest of the people of Yugoslavia and Bosnia."

The one-time enemies met at the Hotel de Marigny state guesthouse opposite the Elysee palace and held an unscheduled second working session after lunch with Chirac and international mediator Carl Bildt.

Sources said the second round of talks was believed to have covered a Bosnian lawsuit against Serbia in the International Court of Justice, France's proposals for a two-year regional stabilisation plan, and the future of the NATO-led IFOR peace force when its mandate expires in December.

Chirac promised that France and the European Union would continue to aid Bosnia's recovery and told Izetbegovic he had "an essential role to play to make peace a success...(and) personify a tolerant Bosnia reconciled at last with itself".

Before their first meeting, the Bosnian and Serbian leaders posed stiffly for photographers at opposite ends of a long Louis XV sofa. They looked more relaxed later, smiling and shaking hands at a joint photo opportunity with Chirac and Bildt in the gardens of the Elysee palace.

Savouring a rare trip outside Serbia in the week that U.N. trade sanctions against rump Yugoslavia were finally lifted, Milosevic took a stroll up the celebrated Champs-Elysees Avenue on Wednesday night to the Arc de Triomphe monument, flanked by two bodyguards and two French security men.

The two presidents signed an agreement in Dayton, Ohio, last November recognizing each other's countries as sovereign states within current borders and agreed "urgently" to establish diplomatic ties and open embassies in each other's capitals.
Sarajevo's lawsuit against Belgrade in March 1993 before the international court in The Hague over alleged Serbian aggression against Bosnia has stalled the process.
The former Yugoslav federal army supported the Bosnian Serbs when they rose against the Bosnian Moslem and Croat bid for independence in 1992.

Milosevic helped secure the Dayton peace accord by forcing recalcitrant Serb leaders to the negotiating table. But the West now expects him to rein in Serb members of the future joint Bosnian government who make no secret of separatist desires.

The West wants the three main players in the Balkan crisis -- Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia -- to normalise relations as soon as possible as a guarantee for stability in the Balkans and a deterrrent against any nationalist drives to break up Bosnia.
Yugoslavia and Croatia recognized each other on August 23.
